# Day 7: Put it together, then retest

**Time:** about 8 minutes, then the retest. **You need:** Everything from this week.

<div class="chang" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Chang Yin</div>

Last day. Short session, then we measure.

Measure twice. Lift once. Warm up with me, then rest five minutes and redo your six tests.
</div>

<div class="box stop" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Stop rule.</span> Stop if you feel chest pain or pressure, dizziness, unusual shortness of breath, or sharp pain. Chest pain, face drooping, arm weakness or trouble speaking? Call 911 now. Pain rule: Mild discomfort up to 3 out of 10 is okay if it settles by tomorrow. Sharper, or worse the next day: back off and ask your doctor or physical therapist.
</div>

## At a glance

| Minutes | Part | Moves |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00–1:30 | Warm-up | Standing march at the counter (45 seconds); Weight shifts (4 shifts each direction) |
| 1:30–8:00 | Full-body round | Chair sit-to-stand (1 set of 8); Wall push-up (1 set of 8); Heel-to-toe stand at the counter (2 holds of 10 seconds each side); One-arm jug row at the counter (1 set of 8 each arm); Heel raises at the counter (1 set of 10); Cyclic sighing (30 seconds) |

## Warm-up (0:00–1:30)

<div class="compact" markdown="1">

### Standing march at the counter

<p class="dose">45 seconds</p>

<a class="pref" href="#ex-standing_march">Same move as before</a>. **Cues:** Stand tall. Knee up, foot down softly. **Breathe:** Breathe steadily. You should be able to talk.

</div>
<table class="eh"><tr><td class="e"><strong>Easier:</strong> Sit and do the seated march.</td><td class="gap"></td><td class="h"><strong>Harder:</strong> Lift knees higher, march faster, or let one hand hover above the counter.</td></tr></table>

<div class="compact" markdown="1">

### Weight shifts

<p class="dose">4 shifts each direction</p>

<a class="pref" href="#ex-weight_shift">Same move as before</a>. **Cues:** Move from your ankles and hips, like a tree swaying. Feet stay flat on the floor. **Breathe:** Breathe slowly.

</div>
<table class="eh"><tr><td class="e"><strong>Easier:</strong> Do it seated: shift your weight side to side on the chair.</td><td class="gap"></td><td class="h"><strong>Harder:</strong> Make the shifts bigger, or let one hand hover.</td></tr></table>

## Full-body round (1:30–8:00)

<div class="compact" markdown="1">

### Chair sit-to-stand

<p class="dose">1 set of 8</p>

<a class="pref" href="#ex-sit_to_stand">Same move as before</a>. **Cues:** Nose over toes. Knees point the same way as your toes. Don't let them cave inward. Sit down slow. Two or three seconds. **Breathe:** Breathe out as you stand. Breathe in as you sit.

</div>
<table class="eh"><tr><td class="e"><strong>Easier:</strong> Put a firm cushion or folded blanket on the seat to make it higher, or push up with your hands on your thighs or on chair arms.</td><td class="gap"></td><td class="h"><strong>Harder:</strong> Arms crossed, lower for a slow count of three, and pause one second just above the seat before touching down. Later: hold a gallon jug of water at your chest.</td></tr></table>

<div class="compact" markdown="1">

### Wall push-up

<p class="dose">1 set of 8</p>

<a class="pref" href="#ex-wall_pushup">Same move as before</a>. **Cues:** Body in one straight line, head to heels. Chest to the wall, not your chin. **Breathe:** Breathe out as you push away.

</div>
<table class="eh"><tr><td class="e"><strong>Easier:</strong> Stand closer to the wall and move only halfway.</td><td class="gap"></td><td class="h"><strong>Harder:</strong> Step your feet farther back. When 15 are easy, move to counter push-ups.</td></tr></table>

<div class="compact" markdown="1">

### Heel-to-toe stand at the counter

<p class="dose">2 holds of 10 seconds each side</p>

<a class="pref" href="#ex-tandem_stand">Same move as before</a>. **Cues:** Eyes on something still at eye level. Soft knees. Tall head. **Breathe:** Breathe slowly and steadily.

**Safety:** Balance drills always start with support. Hands hover, they don't wander away from the counter.

</div>
<table class="eh"><tr><td class="e"><strong>Easier:</strong> Half-step stance: front foot's heel beside the big toe of the back foot. Both hands on the counter.</td><td class="gap"></td><td class="h"><strong>Harder:</strong> Lift one hand to hover just above the counter. Later: both hands hovering.</td></tr></table>

<div class="compact" markdown="1">

### One-arm jug row at the counter

<p class="dose">1 set of 8 each arm</p>

<a class="pref" href="#ex-jug_row">Same move as before</a>. **Cues:** Pull with your elbow, not your hand. Long back. Don't twist. **Breathe:** Breathe out as you pull.

**Safety:** Osteoporosis: keep the hinge small and the back long.

</div>
<table class="eh"><tr><td class="e"><strong>Easier:</strong> Stand upright and pull a towel looped around a sturdy door handle (see Towel row), or use a lighter jug.</td><td class="gap"></td><td class="h"><strong>Harder:</strong> Full gallon jug (about 8 pounds), or a bag with a few cans. Pause for one second at the top.</td></tr></table>

<div class="compact" markdown="1">

### Heel raises at the counter

<p class="dose">1 set of 10</p>

<a class="pref" href="#ex-heel_raise">Same move as before</a>. **Cues:** Tall like someone is pulling a string on top of your head. Weight over the big toe and second toe, not rolling out. **Breathe:** Breathe out as you rise.

**Safety:** Calf cramps are common at first. Stretch and walk them out. One calf that is swollen, red and painful is not a cramp: that is for your doctor, today.

</div>
<table class="eh"><tr><td class="e"><strong>Easier:</strong> Sit in your chair and raise your heels from there, or hold the counter with both hands and rise only halfway.</td><td class="gap"></td><td class="h"><strong>Harder:</strong> One hand on the counter. Later: one leg at a time, with both hands on the counter.</td></tr></table>

<div class="compact" markdown="1">

### Cyclic sighing

<p class="dose">30 seconds</p>

<a class="pref" href="#ex-cyclic_sigh">Same move as before</a>. **Cues:** Two sniffs in, one long sigh out. No holding at any point. **Breathe:** The out-breath is always longer than the in-breath. No breath holds.

**Safety:** If you feel light-headed, return to normal breathing.

</div>
<table class="eh"><tr><td class="e"><strong>Easier:</strong> Just breathe slowly through your nose, making the out-breath a little longer.</td><td class="gap"></td><td class="h"><strong>Harder:</strong> Build up to 5 minutes.</td></tr></table>

<div class="chang" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Chang Yin</div>

You did seven days. Now look at your numbers. Then decide what's next.
</div>

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Today's habit: Call one person.</span> Call someone today and tell them what you did this week. Stronger social ties were linked with a 50% higher likelihood of survival across 148 studies (E37). A link, not a promise. But call anyway.
</div>

# Your seven habit cards

One small habit a day, attached to something you already do. Cut these out and stick today's card on the fridge. By Day 7 you'll have tried all seven. Keep the two you liked best.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Day 1: Sun's protein breakfast.</span> Put 25 to 30 grams of protein in your breakfast (E28). Two eggs plus a cup of soy milk or a small Greek yogurt gets most people there. Kidney disease? Ask your doctor for your number first.

☐ Done today
</div>

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Day 2: Toothbrush balance.</span> While you brush your teeth, stand heel-to-toe with your free hand on the sink or a grab bar. Switch feet halfway. Two minutes, twice a day, is 28 minutes of balance practice a week without trying. Home balance practice is a core part of the Otago programme (E13).

☐ Done today
</div>

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Day 3: Two-bag carry.</span> Every time you bring groceries in, carry two lighter bags, one in each hand, standing tall. It's the carry exercise with a purpose. Pick bags up with a hinge, long back, never a rounded one.

☐ Done today
</div>

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Day 4: After-dinner walk.</span> Walk 10 minutes after your biggest meal. Even 2 to 5 minutes of light walking after eating lowers the blood-sugar rise compared with sitting (E23). Indoors is fine: kitchen to front door, and back.

☐ Done today
</div>

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Day 5: Commercial-break stands.</span> Every time you get up from the sofa or the table, do it twice: stand, sit, then stand. Two extra stands, a dozen times a day, adds up.

☐ Done today
</div>

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Day 6: Five-minute wind-down.</span> Before bed, five minutes of cyclic sighing: two breaths in through the nose, one long breath out through the mouth. In a one-month study of 111 adults, it improved daily mood more than mindfulness meditation (E18). No breath holds.

☐ Done today
</div>

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Day 7: Call one person.</span> Call someone today and tell them what you did this week. Stronger social ties were linked with a 50% higher likelihood of survival across 148 studies (E37). A link, not a promise. But call anyway.

☐ Done today
</div>



# Day 7: the retest

Rest five minutes after today's session. Have some water. Then redo all six tests exactly the way you did on Day 0: same chair, same shoes, same weight for the curl, same helper if you had one. Write the numbers in the Day 7 column of your score sheet, and work out your Strength Age again.

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Sun Yoon. His wife. Also AI. Here's the honest version: in seven days, most of the change is your body getting better at the movement. Your brain learns the move. That's real. Building actual muscle takes weeks of training two or three times a week (E01, E02). So if your number went up one or two, good. If it didn't move, also fine. You started. Seven out of ten. Because I love you.
</div>


**What counts as progress this week:**

- One or two more chair stands. The chair stand is the number that usually moves first.
- A position further on the balance test, or more seconds on the next one.
- The Timed Up and Go a second or two quicker, walking at your normal pace.
- Getting up from the sofa without thinking about it.
- You did seven sessions. That's the habit, and the habit is the program.

**If a number went down:** tired, sore, a bad night's sleep, a different time of day. Retest in a week. If something hurts more than 3 out of 10 and isn't settling, or anything on the red-flag list appears, stop and call your doctor.

# Where the numbers come from

Every number and health statement in this book traces to one of the entries below. They are the same evidence IDs our whole team uses (EVIDENCE.md). Grade A means a Cochrane review, a large meta-analysis or a guideline body. B means a single good trial or a small meta-analysis. C means an observational study: it shows a link, not cause and effect. D means lab, physiology or label data.


<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E01** (grade A). Progressive resistance training in older adults: 121 RCTs, 6,700 people, 2–3×/week. Large effect on strength (SMD 0.84), moderate-to-large effect on getting out of a chair (SMD −0.94), gait speed +0.08 m/s, less osteoarthritis pain. Most side effects were minor soreness or joint pain.

<p class="src">Source: Liu & Latham, Cochrane 2009 — https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD002759_progressive-resistance-strength-training-improving-physical-function-older-adults</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E02** (grade A). NSCA position statement: resistance training is safe and effective for older adults, including frail people. Progress gradually. Train 2–3×/week, 1–3 sets of 6–12 reps at 70–85% 1RM once adapted. Include power (fast lifting intent) and balance.

<p class="src">Source: Fragala et al., J Strength Cond Res 2019 — https://journals.lww.com/nsca-jscr/fulltext/2019/08000/resistance_training_for_older_adults__position.1.aspx</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E03** (grade B (small)). Ten frail nursing-home residents aged ~90, 8 weeks of high-intensity leg training: strength +174%, thigh muscle area up about 9%, walking speed improved. Muscle still adapts in the 90s.

<p class="src">Source: Fiatarone et al., JAMA 1990 — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2342214/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E04** (grade A (review)). Around age 75, muscle mass drops about 0.6–1% per year while strength drops 2.5–4% per year. Strength declines 2–5× faster than mass.

<p class="src">Source: Mitchell et al., Frontiers in Physiology 2012 — https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2012.00260/full</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E05** (grade B). 10 days of bed rest in healthy adults (mean age 67) cost about 0.95 kg of leg lean mass, with muscle protein synthesis down about 30%. Younger adults lost under 0.4 kg over 28 days.

<p class="src">Source: Kortebein et al., JAMA 2007 — https://news.uams.edu/2007/04/25/extended-bed-rest-accelerates-muscle-deterioration-in-older-adults-uams-researchers-report-in-jama/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E06** (grade A (consensus)). Sarcopenia screening cut-offs (EWGSOP2): grip under 27 kg for men or under 16 kg for women, or 5 chair rises taking more than 15 s, signals "probable sarcopenia".

<p class="src">Source: Cruz-Jentoft et al., Age Ageing 2019 — https://www.esceo.org/sites/esceo/files/pdf/2019%20Age%20Ageing%20EWGSOP2.pdf</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E07** (grade C). PURE study: 142,861 adults in 17 countries. Every 5 kg lower grip strength was linked with 16% higher all-cause mortality and 17% higher CV mortality. Grip predicted mortality better than systolic blood pressure.

<p class="src">Source: Leong et al., Lancet 2015 — https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(14)62000-6/abstract ; summary https://www.consultant360.com/exclusives/could-grip-strength-predict-all-cause-mortality-risk</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E09** (grade C). 10-second one-leg stance (free foot resting on the back of the other calf, arms at sides, 3 tries). 1,702 people aged 51–75. Failing it was linked with 84% higher all-cause mortality over about 7 years. Failure rates: about 18% at 61–65, about 37% at 66–70, over 50% at 71–75.

<p class="src">Source: Araújo et al., BJSM 2022 — https://www.bristol.ac.uk/news/2022/june/tne-second-one-legged-stance.html</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E10** (grade C). Gait speed and survival: 34,485 adults 65+. 0.8 m/s is around median life expectancy. ≥1.0 m/s was linked with longer-than-expected survival. Under 0.6 m/s means higher risk.

<p class="src">Source: Studenski et al., JAMA 2011 — https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2011/01/110104161621.htm</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E11** (grade A (tool)). CDC STEADI 30-second chair stand (17-inch chair, arms crossed), used in the CDC's older-adult screening. Below-average scores: men 60–64 <14, 65–69 <12, 70–74 <12, 75–79 <11, 80–84 <10, 85–89 <8, 90–94 <7. Women 60–64 <12, 65–69 <11, 70–74 <10, 75–79 <10, 80–84 <9, 85–89 <8, 90–94 <4. If arms are used to stand, the score is 0.

<p class="src">Source: CDC STEADI — https://www.cdc.gov/steadi/media/pdfs/STEADI-Assessment-30Sec-508.pdf</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E13** (grade A−). Otago Exercise Programme: a home programme of leg strengthening, balance exercises and walking designed for older adults, studied in 7 trials with 1,503 people (mean age 81.6). We use its exercise types and progressions; we make no outcome claim from it.

<p class="src">Source: Thomas et al., Age Ageing 2010 — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK78898/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E15** (grade B+). Tai chi vs physical therapy for knee osteoarthritis: 204 adults. Similar improvements in pain and function at 12 weeks, sustained to 52 weeks. Tai chi group had more improvement in depression and quality of life.

<p class="src">Source: Wang et al., Ann Intern Med 2016 — https://www.nccih.nih.gov/research/research-results/study-shows-tai-chi-and-physical-therapy-were-equally-helpful-for-knee-osteoarthritis</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E17** (grade A−). Baduanjin/qigong in older adults: meta-analyses report better sleep quality and fewer depressive symptoms (moderate certainty, heterogeneous trials).

<p class="src">Source: Frontiers Public Health 2026 meta-analysis — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13501274/ ; qigong & sleep meta — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12757222/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E18** (grade B). 111 adults, 5 min/day for 1 month. Cyclic sighing (two inhales through the nose, long slow exhale through the mouth) produced the largest daily improvement in positive mood, more than mindfulness meditation. All breathing groups improved.

<p class="src">Source: Balban et al., Cell Reports Medicine 2023 — https://stanmed.stanford.edu/cyclic-sighing-stress-relief/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E19** (grade A− (meta)). Voluntary slow breathing (around 6 breaths/min) increases vagally-mediated heart-rate variability during and after practice.

<p class="src">Source: Laborde et al., Neurosci Biobehav Rev 2022 — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0149763422002007</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E20** (grade A). Exercise and resting BP: 270 RCTs, 15,827 people. Isometric training lowered BP the most (−8.24/−4.00 mmHg). Wall squat ranked top for systolic. Aerobic −4.49/−2.53, dynamic resistance −4.55/−3.04. These are average changes over weeks of training, not instant.

<p class="src">Source: Edwards et al., BJSM 2023 — https://bmjgroup.com/static-isometric-exercise-such-as-wall-sits-best-for-lowering-blood-pressure/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E22** (grade C). Daily steps: in adults 60+, mortality benefit plateaued at about 6,000–8,000 steps/day. The top quartiles had 40–53% lower risk than the lowest (about 3,500/day).

<p class="src">Source: Paluch et al., Lancet Public Health 2022 — https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2022/03/220303112207.htm</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E23** (grade A− (meta)). Light walking after meals (even 2–5 minutes) lowers the post-meal glucose rise compared with sitting.

<p class="src">Source: Buffey et al., Sports Med 2022 — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35147898/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E28** (grade A (consensus)). PROT-AGE: adults over 65 should get 1.0–1.2 g protein/kg/day, and 1.2–1.5 g/kg if active or ill (unless there is severe kidney disease). Aim for 25–30 g per meal with about 2.5–2.8 g leucine.

<p class="src">Source: Bauer et al., JAMDA 2013 — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23867520/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E30** (grade A). Exercise for chronic low back pain: 249 trials, 24,486 people. Pain about 15 points better (0–100 scale) at 3 months vs no treatment or usual care. Function improved modestly.

<p class="src">Source: Hayden et al., Cochrane 2021 — https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD009790_exercise-treatment-chronic-low-back-pain</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E37** (grade C (meta of cohorts)). 148 studies, 308,849 people. Stronger social relationships were linked with a 50% higher likelihood of survival (OR 1.50), comparable to well-known risk factors like smoking.

<p class="src">Source: Holt-Lunstad et al., PLoS Med 2010 — https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pmed.1000316</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E39** (grade A−). High-velocity "power" training (lift with fast intent, lower slowly) gives functional gains similar to or slightly better than traditional training in older adults, and it is safe when supervised and progressed.

<p class="src">Source: J Physiotherapy 2023 systematic review — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S183695532300053X ; Eur Rev Aging Phys Act 2022 — https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s11556-022-00297-x</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E40** (grade A (consensus)). Osteoporosis exercise guidance: do resistance and balance training. Avoid rapid, repeated or loaded spinal flexion (sit-ups, toe-touches with weight) and forceful twisting. Flexion-exercise programs were linked with more vertebral fractures.

<p class="src">Source: Giangregorio et al., "Too Fit To Fracture", Osteoporos Int 2014 — https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00198-014-2881-4 ; Sinaki & Mikkelsen, Arch Phys Med Rehabil 1984</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E41** (grade B (known literature)). Pain-monitoring model: during and after exercise, pain up to about 3/10 (we use a conservative threshold) is acceptable if it settles by the next morning and isn't trending up week to week.

<p class="src">Source: Thomeé, Phys Ther 1997; Silbernagel et al., Am J Sports Med 2007</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E42** (grade A (statement)). AHA scientific statement (2023): resistance training is recommended for adults with and without cardiovascular disease. It lowers blood pressure and improves glucose control and function. Avoid breath-holding (Valsalva). People with CVD should get individualized clearance.

<p class="src">Source: Paluch et al., Circulation 2024 — https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001189</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E43** (grade A (guideline)). Pre-exercise screening (ACSM 2015): anyone with symptoms of cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease (chest pain, unusual breathlessness, fainting) should get medical clearance before starting. Otherwise, light-to-moderate exercise can begin and progress.

<p class="src">Source: Riebe et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc 2015 (known literature)</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E46** (grade A− (meta, known literature)). Orthostatic hypotension (a blood-pressure drop on standing) is common in older adults. A meta-analysis found it in about 22% of community-dwelling older people. The risk is higher with some blood-pressure and other medicines. Practical rule: sit, pump your ankles, then stand slowly while holding something.

<p class="src">Source: Saedon et al., J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2020 (prevalence of orthostatic hypotension, systematic review & meta-analysis)</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E47** (grade D (physiology)). The calf muscle pump: calf contraction compresses the deep veins and, with the venous valves, pushes blood back toward the heart. It's standard physiology. Walking and heel raises activate it. A red flag is one swollen, red, painful calf (possible clot), which needs a doctor, not exercise.

<p class="src">Source: Standard physiology texts; e.g. Recek, Int J Angiol 2013 "Calf pump activity influencing venous hemodynamics in the lower extremity" (known literature)</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E49** (grade A (tool/norms)). Senior Fitness Test (Rikli & Jones): 7,183 US community-dwelling adults aged 60–94 from 267 sites in 21 states. "Normal range" = the middle 50% (25th–75th percentile) for each 5-year age band and sex. 30-s chair stand, 30-s arm curl (5 lb women / 8 lb men), 2-minute step test (right-knee lifts to midway between kneecap and hip bone), chair sit-and-reach (inches, + past the toes / − short of them). Example normal ranges, women 70–74: chair stand 10–15, arm curl 12–17, step test 68–101, sit-and-reach −1.0 to +4.0 in; men 70–74: 12–17, 14–21, 80–110, −3.5 to +2.5 in. Full tables in products/strength_reset.md. It's a fitness comparison, not a diagnosis.

<p class="src">Source: Rikli & Jones, Senior Fitness Test Manual, 2nd ed. 2013 (primary not opened). Opened: normative tables — https://integrativephysicaltherapyservices.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/Fitness-Testing-for-Seniors-PDF.pdf ; protocol + sample size — https://fitnessnorms.com/functional/chair-sit-and-reach/ , https://fitnessnorms.com/functional/step-test/ , https://fitnessnorms.com/functional/arm-curl/ . Note: the PDF's women 60–64 sit-and-reach cell reads "−0.5 to +0.5" (typo); we use the fitnessnorms 25th–75th percentiles (−0.6 to +4.8 in).</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E50** (grade A (tool)). CDC STEADI 4-Stage Balance Test: feet side by side, semi-tandem (instep beside big toe), tandem (heel to toe), one leg; up to 10 s each, stop at the first stage not held. The CDC uses the tandem stand as a screening checkpoint: under 10 s is worth discussing with a clinician.

<p class="src">Source: CDC STEADI — opened https://www.cdc.gov/steadi/media/pdfs/STEADI-Assessment-4Stage-508.pdf</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E51** (grade A (tool)). CDC STEADI Timed Up and Go: stand from a chair, walk 10 feet (3 m) at normal pace, turn, walk back, sit. The CDC uses 12 seconds or more as a screening threshold worth discussing with a clinician. Always have someone stand by.

<p class="src">Source: CDC STEADI — opened https://www.cdc.gov/steadi/media/pdfs/STEADI-Assessment-TUG-508.pdf</p>

</div>
